title: "Do the three contraceptive methods differ in community composition?"

  html:

> Sub-question 1 (microbiome column). 93 women, one sample each, chose one
> of three methods: injectable (39), pill (28), ring (26). Nobody was
> randomised, so any difference we see is an association, not proof the
> method caused it.
>
> Pipeline: `tax_transform() |> dist_calc() |> ord_calc("PCoA") |> ord_plot()`

```{r setup}
library(conflicted)  # make any name clash between packages a loud error
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(microViz)
library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)

# filter() is claimed by both dplyr and base R. We always mean the dplyr one.
conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)

source(here("R/count_tables.R"))

# Species seen in at least 10 of the 93 samples; rarer ones are mostly noise.
ps <- as_counts(dataset = "group_b", table = "microbiome",
                min_count = 1, min_samples = 10)
ps
```

## The ordination

Bray-Curtis on relative abundance (compositional transform) — the version
we learned on Tuesday. Each point is one person, coloured by method.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
ord_bray <- ps |>
  tax_transform("compositional") |>
  dist_calc("bray") |>
  ord_calc("PCoA")

p_pcoa <- ord_bray |>
  ord_plot(colour = "arm") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = arm), type = "t", linetype = 2) +
  labs(title = "Bray-Curtis PCoA, coloured by method")
p_pcoa

# Save a copy for the group's slides.
dir.create(here("group_project/figures"), showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(here("group_project/figures/pcoa-by-arm.png"),
       plot = p_pcoa, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

The same points coloured by BV status and pH, to see what *else* axis 1 or
axis 2 might be tracking:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
ord_bray |>
  ord_plot(colour = "bv") +
  labs(title = "Same ordination, coloured by Amsel BV status") ->
  p_bv
ord_bray |>
  ord_plot(colour = "ph") +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "Same ordination, coloured by pH") ->
  p_ph
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_bv, p_ph, nrow = 1)
```

## Is the difference real, and is it a centre or a spread?

PERMANOVA asks: could a distance matrix this structured arise if the
method labels were shuffled? We use `by = "margin"` because the arms were
not randomised and differ in pH and BV, so the variables are entangled.

```{r}
dist_bray <- ord_bray |> dist_get()
meta <- as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame")

vegan::adonis2(dist_bray ~ arm + bv + ph + any_sti, data = meta,
               permutations = 999, by = "margin")
```

PERMANOVA can be significant because groups sit in different **places**
(centroids) or just have different **spreads**. This test separates the two:

```{r}
vegan::betadisper(as.dist(dist_bray), meta$arm) |> permutest()
```

## A second distance, to check the answer isn't a fluke of Bray-Curtis

CLR (centred log ratio) + Euclidean is the Aitchison distance: it treats
the data as compositional from the start rather than just converting to
percentages.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
ord_clr <- ps |>
  tax_transform("clr") |>
  dist_calc("euclidean") |>
  ord_calc("PCoA")

ord_clr |>
  ord_plot(colour = "arm") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = arm), type = "t", linetype = 2) +
  labs(title = "CLR + Euclidean PCoA (Aitchison)")

vegan::adonis2(ord_clr |> dist_get() ~ arm + bv + ph + any_sti,
               data = meta, permutations = 999, by = "margin")
```

## Which comparisons are actually powered?

With 93 people in three unequal arms, a two-arm contrast is better powered
than the three-way test. Ring (26) versus the two systemic methods pooled
(67) is our best-powered comparison:

```{r}
meta_ring <- meta |> mutate(systemic = arm != "ring")
vegan::adonis2(dist_bray ~ systemic + bv + ph + any_sti, data = meta_ring,
               permutations = 999, by = "margin")
```

## What tracks the ordination axes?

The genera most correlated with axis 1, so the difference has a face:

```{r}
ps |>
  tax_agg("Genus") |>
  tax_transform("compositional") |>
  dist_calc("bray") |>
  ord_calc("PCoA") |>
  ord_plot(colour = "arm", plot_taxa = 8,
           tax_vec_length = 1) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = arm), type = "t", linetype = 2) +
  labs(title = "Which genera point along the axes?")
```

The arrows are the eight most abundant genera; an arrow pointing the same way
as a cluster of points means that genus is more abundant in those samples.

The number behind the picture: correlation of each genus's relative
abundance with axis 1 (Spearman, which copes with the many zeros).

```{r}
# Axis scores: one MDS1/MDS2 pair per sample, from the ordination object
sc <- vegan::scores(ord_bray@ord, display = "sites")[, 1:2]

# Genus-level relative abundances (taxa in rows, samples in columns)
ps_genus <- ps |> tax_agg("Genus") |> tax_transform("compositional")
genus_rel <- t(as.matrix(ps_genus@counts))
stopifnot(identical(colnames(genus_rel), rownames(sc)))  # same samples, same order

cors <- apply(genus_rel, 1, \(g) cor(g, sc[, 1], method = "spearman"))
tibble(taxon = names(cors), spearman_with_axis1 = round(cors, 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(spearman_with_axis1))) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)
```

## Interpretation

- **The three methods do not detectably differ in community composition.**
  The three-way PERMANOVA gives arm p = 0.075 (R² = 2.8%) once BV, pH and
  STI are in the model, and the best-powered contrast, ring vs systemic
  pooled, is clearly null (p = 0.85). Alpha diversity agrees: Shannon by
  arm was not significant either (p = 0.47).
- **What does differ is BV status: R² = 14%, p = 0.001** — five times more
  of the variation than the method explains. Axis 1 is essentially a BV
  axis: Gardnerella, Dialister, Prevotella, Sneathia and Fannyhessea load
  positive, *Lactobacillus* strongly negative. The ellipses overlap by arm
  but separate by BV in the second ordination plot.
- The difference is a **shift, not a spread**: betadisper p = 0.77, so the
  three arms are equally dispersed and the (weak) arm signal is not a
  heterogeneity artifact.
- **BV is a plausible confounder, not just a covariate.** Nobody was
  randomised, and BV is not distributed evenly across arms (QC report:
  10/26 ring positive vs 29/67 systemic), so part of what looks like a
  method effect could be who chose which method. With `by = "margin"` the
  arm effect is what is left *after* crediting BV — and what is left is
  very little.
- **What we can and cannot claim:** with 93 people in arms of 26 to 39, we
  are underpowered for small shifts. We can rule out a *large* method
  effect on composition; a small one could hide inside p = 0.075. This
  links straight to the connecting-the-two question: if BV explains the
  composition, does it also explain any gene-expression differences?

## Choices made

- Ordinated on species seen in ≥10 of 93 samples; alternative was no
  filter, which lets single-sample species add noise to every distance.
- Main distance is **Bray-Curtis on relative abundance**; alternative was
  Jaccard (presence/absence), which ignores how abundant anything is.
- Added **CLR + Euclidean** as a second opinion; alternative was to trust
  one distance only.
- PERMANOVA with `by = "margin"` because arm, BV, pH and STI are
  entangled in an observational design; alternative was `by = "terms"`,
  which credits each variable in the order entered.
- Tested dispersion with `betadisper` before trusting a significant
  PERMANOVA; alternative was to report R² without checking spread.
- Pooled the two systemic methods to compare against the ring for power;
  alternative was all pairwise tests, which triples the number of tests.
